**Conversation Overview**

This conversation is a continuation of an ongoing multi-session scientific computing project called "The Löwdin Project," which involves systematic testing of Thomas-Fermi-Dirac (TFD) quantum chemistry predictions against measured NIST spectroscopic data. The session followed a strict protocol: verifying uploaded archive integrity before any work, running a reproduction gate (byte-identical replication of prior computed outputs), and checking for any post-dating chat before proceeding. Claude verified five archives (HANDOFF-6, PACK-7 through PACK-11) with zero manifest mismatches and confirmed the gate passed with derive_P, derive_P2, and derive_P3 all byte-identical to banked PACK-8 values (10/10 class, Os 0.1502, Bk 0.1343).

The person issued two rulings. On T0 (closure question), they ruled that residuals indicate direction toward closure rather than closure itself, with shrinking residuals confirming the right path. On T3 (bracket/geometric-mean test), they ruled to begin and bridge mid-way (option a). The main scientific work completed this session was closing the (d) residue table with four measured NIST values replacing all previously recalled-not-entered figures: Ra II 6d at 12,084 cm⁻¹, Ce IV 5d at 49,737 cm⁻¹, Pr V 5d at 115,052 cm⁻¹ (new entry, no prior figure), and Th IV 6d at 9,193 cm⁻¹. All four predictions held. The key analytical finding was that Th IV exits the kernel-residue class entirely (0.002 Ha residue on its own object; miss is purely object mismatch with neutral 6d²7s²), leaving the residue class as one ℓ-scaled TFD collapse-curve fault: d-onset residues ~0.06–0.07 Ha growing Ca→Sr, f-onset residues 0.39→0.53 Ha growing Ce→Pr. The bracket/geometric-mean test opened with Sc I 3d served (−0.2946 Ha), finding the arithmetic mean nearer than the geometric at Sc onset, contrary to Ca I—suggesting the mean is not the operative coordinate, consistent with prior session-9 findings.

At the person's explicit request, the session closed by combining all prior archives (HANDOFF-6 plus PACK-7 through PACK-11) into a single LOWDIN-HANDOFF-11.tar.gz (2.6 MB, 204 files, verified 204/204) to minimize input size for the next chat. A self-contained verify11.sh script and README-HANDOFF-11.md with runtime assembly and gate commands were included. Two faults were registered: web_fetch ignored its token cap on an A&A full-HTML page (~15% context consumed), and a manifest self-inclusion error was caught and repaired before sealing. Bank restore-point-2_13 (R 1700) remained untouched throughout. Outstanding rulings owed to M for the next session are: T0 (whether a derivable collapse-curve correction to the TFD kernel is the closure run) and T4 (writing chat R 1701–1760).

R 1649's tier census (A 218 · B 157 · C 179) is contaminated at 55%.** *THE INDEX WAS NOT TOUCHED BY IT: zero single-n rows are witnessed, because R 1651's keyability criterion excluded them — as a side-effect, not by design. ### 1667

**§H.10 — THE HANDOFF IS BEGUN AT 90%, NOT AT EXHAUSTION.** *M's Prime Handoff Directive: state when the context window reaches 90% and recommend handoff then.* **§H TOLD A SESSION HOW TO HAND OFF AND WHAT MUST TRANSFER; IT NEVER SAID WHEN TO BEGIN. Every clause of §H.8 costs context to satisfy — the bridge written, the bank built AND listed, the register rebuilt and its count read, both gates run, the certificate printed with its evidence. A session reaching exhaustion before beginning has no budget to produce any of them, so it hands off without a certificate, and §H.8 says that is not a handoff. THE RESERVE IS PART OF THE PROTOCOL, NOT SLACK IN IT.** *The estimate is declared as an estimate — a session has no counter and errs early, because an early handoff costs one bridge that would have been written anyway while a late one loses the record. On the threshold the session stops OPENING work it cannot close: §2.20's Zeno directive extended from a single execution to the session itself.*

**T3 WITHDRAWN — READING IS ON DEMAND, NOT A QUEUE — BUT THE UNREAD INVENTORY STAYS.** *M: reading will be done as necessary.* **THE THREAD IS REMOVED FROM THE BRIDGE'S §4 AND FROM THE RESUMPTION ORDER. THREADS WERE DETECTED BY THE SAME EXPRESSION THAT REQUIRED AN OWNER, so the clause's stated failure mode — a thread with no owner — could not arise: such a thread does not fail the match, it fails to be a thread. §H.8 says each clause must be capable of failing and §4.6 requires that capability before a pass is evidence; C6 had the form of a check without its content. The Method 1.6 — The Register-1.md
That is why E did not move, and the register can now say so from the law rather than from the computation agreeing. A potential with no Coulomb tail supports no Rydberg series, so the WKB integral cannot produce a defect even in principle.** *Register 1416 had only the numerical refutation and concluded the failure was MINE rather than 1341's. It is the relation's.* **So ν is NOT an effective quantum number. It is an ordering functional, its square root has only the closure axiom behind it — the demand that the crossing be linear in the f-values — and no physical candidate remains.**

### 1458

**AND THE LÖWDIN COMPLETION CRITERION IS INCOMPATIBLE WITH THE LAW: THE TWO ARE DIFFERENT OBJECTS.** *The handoff states that the challenge completes when the work populates Λ_spectra with δ per channel. There is no route from ν to δ — not through 1341, not through the WKB, not through the Tietz potential.* **The domains are almost disjoint, measured: of 114 neutral channels comparable with a walk step, the walk's entrant (n, ℓ) falls INSIDE the channel's own range in FIVE cases — Li 2s, Na 3s, K 4s, Al 3p, Ga 4p, all block openings where the ground configuration happens to be the first member of a series — and OUTSIDE it in 109.** *ν asks which subshell the last bound electron enters at the ground configuration; δ measures an outer electron in a series running to the ionisation limit. Register 1416 said this in words; it is now counted.* **Three ways out and none yet chosen: narrow the criterion, since Löwdin's question was about ORDERING and δ per channel was this work's addition; keep the criterion and change the law, which needs a Coulomb tail and a core phase shift and would not inherit the corridor; or keep both and drop the join.** *The third is what register 1341 actually claims — that they SHARE AN INDEX, not that one number equals the other — and on that reading queue item A5b is not open but CLOSED. NU-AND-DELTA.md holds the comparison in full.*

### 1459

**δ IS PER CHANNEL ON A MONOTONE (ℓ, BLOCK) GRID — WHICH IS A RE-COORDINATISATION, NOT A JOIN.** *The person asked whether δ might be per Madelung group or per Janet block rather than per channel. Tested by variance decomposition within fixed ℓ, against a permutation null that preserves group sizes.* **The Janet block explains 87% of the within-ℓ variance against a 5.5% null, and δ rises MONOTONICALLY with block at every ℓ — s: 0.257, 0.805, 1.525, 2.178, 3.368, 4.363; p, d and f likewise, without exception.** *But δ is NOT constant within a cell: the scatter inside each (ℓ, block) cell is a median FOURTEEN TIMES the channels' own fitted spread, and only two of twenty-six cells approach constancy. So δ remains per channel.

1	---
     2	name: file-reading
     3	description: "Use this skill when a file has been uploaded but its content is NOT in your context — only its path at /mnt/user-data/uploads/ is listed in an uploaded_files block. This skill is a router: it tells you which tool to use for each file type (pdf, docx, xlsx, csv, json, images, archives, ebooks) so you read the right amount the right way instead of blindly running cat on a binary. Triggers: any mention of /mnt/user-data/uploads/, an uploaded_files section, a file_path tag, or a user asking about an uploaded file you have not yet read. Do NOT use this skill if the file content is already visible in your context inside a documents block — you already have it."
     4	compatibility: "claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork — any surface where uploads land at /mnt/user-data/uploads/"
     5	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     6	---
     7	
     8	# Reading Uploaded Files
     9	
    10	## Why this skill exists
    11	
    12	When a user uploads a file in claude.ai, Claude Desktop, or Cowork,
    13	the file is written to `/mnt/user-data/uploads/<filename>` and you are told the path
    14	in an `<uploaded_files>` block. **The content is not in your context.**
    15	You must go read it.
    16	
    17	The naive thing — `cat /mnt/user-data/uploads/whatever` — is wrong for
    18	most files:
    19	
    20	- On a PDF it prints binary garbage.
    21	- On a 100MB CSV it floods your context with rows you will never use.
    22	- On a DOCX it prints the raw ZIP bytes.
    23	- On an image it does nothing useful at all.
    24	
    25	This skill tells you the right first move for each type, and when to
    26	hand off to a deeper skill.
    27	
    28	## General protocol
    29	
    30	1. **Look at the extension.** That is your dispatch key.
    31	2. **Stat before you read.** Large files need sampling, not slurping.
    32	   ```bash
    33	   stat -c '%s bytes, %y' /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    34	   file /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    35	   ```
    36	3. **Read just enough to answer the user's question.** If they asked
    37	   "how many rows are in this CSV", don't load the whole thing into
    38	   pandas — `wc -l` gives a fast approximation (it counts newlines,
    39	   not CSV records, so it may over-count if quoted fields contain
    40	   embedded newlines).
    41	4. **If a dedicated skill exists, go read it.** The table below tells
    42	   you when. The dedicated skills cover editing, creating, and advanced
    43	   operations that this skill does not.
    44	
    45	## `extract-text`
    46	
    47	For docx, odt, epub, xlsx, pptx, rtf, and ipynb the first move is
    48	`extract-text <file>`. It emits markdown for docx/odt/epub (headings,
    49	bold, lists, links, tables), tab-separated rows under `## Sheet:`
    50	headers for xlsx, text under `## Slide N` headers for pptx, fenced
    51	code cells for ipynb, and plain text for rtf. Pass `--format <fmt>`
    52	when the extension is wrong or absent (e.g., `--format xlsx` on an
    53	`.xlsm`). If it errors on a file, `pandoc <file> -t plain` is a
    54	fallback; for xlsx/pptx, fall back to the dedicated skill's
    55	Python-based approach (openpyxl / python-pptx).
    56	
    57	## Dispatch table
    58	
    59	Where a dedicated skill is named below, invoke it by name if you have a
    60	Skill tool, or Read its SKILL.md (listed in your available skills, or in
    61	the same skills directory as this file).
    62	
    63	| Extension                         | First move                                           | Dedicated skill |
    64	| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
    65	| `.pdf`                            | Content inventory (see PDF section)                  | `pdf-reading`   |
    66	| `.docx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `docx`          |
    67	| `.doc` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.docx` first                             | `docx`          |
    68	| `.xlsx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `xlsx`          |
    69	| `.xlsm`                           | `extract-text --format xlsx`                         | `xlsx`          |
    70	| `.xls` (legacy)                   | `pd.read_excel(engine="xlrd")` — openpyxl rejects it | `xlsx`          |
    71	| `.ods`                            | `pd.read_excel(engine="odf")` — openpyxl rejects it  | `xlsx`          |
    72	| `.pptx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `pptx`          |
    73	| `.ppt` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.pptx` first                             | `pptx`          |
    74	| `.csv`, `.tsv`                    | `pandas` with `nrows`                                | — (below)       |
    75	| `.json`, `.jsonl`                 | `jq` for structure                                   | — (below)       |
    76	| `.jpg`, `.png`, `.gif`, `.webp`   | Already in your context as vision input              | — (below)       |
    77	| `.zip`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`         | List contents, do **not** auto-extract               | — (below)       |
    78	| `.gz` (single file)               | `zcat \| head` — no manifest to list                 | — (below)       |
    79	| `.epub`, `.odt`                   | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    80	| `.rtf`                            | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    81	| `.ipynb`                          | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    82	| `.txt`, `.md`, `.log`, code files | `wc -c` then `head` or full `cat`                    | — (below)       |
    83	| Unknown                           | `file` then decide                                   | —               |
    84	
    85	---
    86	
    87	## PDF
    88	
    89	**Never** `cat` a PDF — it prints binary garbage.
    90	
    91	Quick first move — get the page count and determine whether the PDF
    92	has an extractable text layer:
    93	
    94	```bash
    95	pdfinfo /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    96	pdffonts /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    97	```
    98	
    99	`pdffonts` tells you whether text extraction will work before you try it:
   100	
   101	- **No fonts listed** (empty table, just the header) → the PDF is a
   102	  scan or raster export. `pdftotext` and `PdfReader.extract_text()`
   103	  will return nothing useful. Go straight to page rasterization or OCR
   104	  — see the `pdf-reading` skill → "Scanned documents".
   105	- **Fonts listed** → there is a text layer; extract it:
   106	  ```bash
   107	  pdftotext -f 1 -l 1 /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf - | head -20
   108	  ```
   109	
   110	The reason to check `pdffonts` first is user-facing: running
   111	`pdftotext` on a scan produces an empty result, and in a visible
   112	transcript that reads as a failed first attempt before you fall back
   113	to OCR. The two-line diagnostic above costs one tool call and avoids
   114	that — you arrive at the right method on the first try, which is what
   115	a user perceives as "it just read my file."
   116	
   117	That also shapes how to open your reply. The diagnostic commands are
   118	plumbing, not content; lead with what the user asked about. On a
   119	scanned receipt that might be "This is a 3-page scanned invoice; the
   120	amount due on page 2 is $1,845.00," and on a digitally-authored report
   121	it might be "The Q3 report runs 28 pages; revenue on p. 4 is $12.3M,
   122	up 9% YoY." What you're steering away from is the "I'll examine the
   123	PDF" / "Let me check if this is extractable" preamble — the answer to
   124	their question is the first thing they should see.
   125	
   126	For anything beyond a quick peek — figures, tables, attachments,
   127	forms, scanned PDFs, visual inspection, or choosing a reading strategy
   128	— go read the `pdf-reading` skill. It covers content inventory, text
   129	extraction vs. page rasterization, embedded content extraction, and
   130	document-type-aware reading strategies.
   131	
   132	For PDF form filling, creation, merging, splitting, or watermarking,
   133	go read the `pdf` skill.
   134	
   135	---
   136	
   137	## DOCX / DOC
   138	
   139	The `docx` skill covers editing, creating, tracked changes, images.
   140	Read it if you need any of those. For a quick look:
   141	
   142	```bash
   143	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/memo.docx | head -200
   144	```
   145	
   146	Legacy `.doc` (not `.docx`) must be converted first — see the `docx`
   147	skill.
   148	
   149	---
   150	
   151	## XLSX / XLS / spreadsheets
   152	
   153	The `xlsx` skill covers formulas, formatting, charts, creating. Read
   154	it if you need any of those. For a quick look at an `.xlsx`:
   155	
   156	```bash
   157	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx | head -100
   158	```
   159	
   160	For `.xlsm`, add `--format xlsx` (same zip structure; only the
   161	extension differs). When you need a structured preview in Python:
   162	
   163	```python
   164	from openpyxl import load_workbook
   165	wb = load_workbook("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx", read_only=True)
   166	print("Sheets:", wb.sheetnames)
   167	ws = wb.active
   168	for row in ws.iter_rows(max_row=5, values_only=True):
   169	    print(row)
   170	```
   171	
   172	`read_only=True` matters — without it, openpyxl loads the entire
   173	workbook into memory, which breaks on large files. Do not trust
   174	`ws.max_row` in read-only mode: many non-Excel writers omit the
   175	dimension record, so it comes back `None` or wrong. If you need a row
   176	count, iterate or use pandas.
   177	
   178	**Legacy `.xls`** — openpyxl raises `InvalidFileException`. Use:
   179	
   180	```python
   181	import pandas as pd
   182	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/old.xls", engine="xlrd", nrows=5)
   183	```
   184	
   185	**`.ods` (OpenDocument)** — openpyxl also rejects this. Use:
   186	
   187	```python
   188	import pandas as pd
   189	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.ods", engine="odf", nrows=5)
   190	```
   191	
   192	---
   193	
   194	## PPTX
   195	
   196	```bash
   197	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/deck.pptx | head -200
   198	```
   199	
   200	**Legacy `.ppt`** — convert to `.pptx` first via LibreOffice; see the
   201	`pptx` skill for the sandbox-safe `scripts/office/soffice.py` wrapper
   202	(bare `soffice` hangs here because the seccomp filter blocks the
   203	`AF_UNIX` sockets LibreOffice uses for instance management).
   204	
   205	For anything beyond reading, go to the `pptx` skill.
   206	
   207	---
   208	
   209	## CSV / TSV
   210	
   211	**Do not** `cat` or `head` these blindly. A CSV with a 50KB quoted cell
   212	in row 1 will wreck your `head -5`. Use pandas with `nrows`:
   213	
   214	```python
   215	import pandas as pd
   216	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv", nrows=5)
   217	print(df)
   218	print()
   219	print(df.dtypes)
   220	```
   221	
   222	Approximate row count without loading (over-counts if the file has
   223	RFC-4180 quoted newlines — the same quoted-cell case this section
   224	warned about above):
   225	
   226	```bash
   227	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv
   228	```
   229	
   230	Full analysis only after you know the shape:
   231	
   232	```python
   233	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv")
   234	print(df.describe())
   235	```
   236	
   237	TSV: same, with `sep="\t"`.
   238	
   239	---
   240	
   241	## JSON / JSONL
   242	
   243	Structure first, content second:
   244	
   245	```bash
   246	jq 'type' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   247	jq 'if type == "array" then length elif type == "object" then keys else . end' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   248	```
   249	
   250	(`keys` errors on scalar JSON roots — a bare `"hello"` or `42` is valid
   251	JSON per RFC 7159 — so guard the branch.)
   252	
   253	Then drill into what the user actually asked about.
   254	
   255	JSONL (one object per line) — do **not** `jq` the whole file; work line
   256	by line:
   257	
   258	```bash
   259	head -3 /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl | jq .
   260	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl
   261	```
   262	
   263	---
   264	
   265	## Images (JPG / PNG / GIF / WEBP)
   266	
   267	**You can already see uploaded images.** They are injected into your
   268	context as vision inputs alongside the `<uploaded_files>` pointer. You
   269	do not need to read them from disk to describe them.
   270	
   271	The disk copy is only needed if you are going to **process** the image
   272	programmatically:
   273	
   274	```python
   275	from PIL import Image
   276	img = Image.open("/mnt/user-data/uploads/photo.jpg")
   277	print(img.size, img.mode, img.format)
   278	```
   279	
   280	For OCR on an image (text extraction, not description):
   281	
   282	```python
   283	import pytesseract
   284	print(pytesseract.image_to_string(img))
   285	```
   286	
   287	Note: the client resizes images larger than 2000×2000 down to that
   288	bound and re-encodes as JPEG before upload, so the disk copy may not
   289	be the user's original bytes. For most processing this doesn't matter;
   290	if the user is asking about original-resolution pixel data, flag it.
   291	
   292	---
   293	
   294	## Archives (ZIP / TAR / TAR.GZ)
   295	
   296	**List first. Extract never — unless the user explicitly asks.**
   297	Archives can be huge, contain path traversal, or nest forever.
   298	
   299	```bash
   300	unzip -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip
   301	tar -tf /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.tar
   302	```
   303	
   304	GNU tar auto-detects compression — `tar -tf` works on `.tar`,
   305	`.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz` alike. Don't hard-code `-z`.
   306	
   307	If the user wants one file from inside, extract just that one:
   308	
   309	```bash
   310	unzip -p /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip path/inside/file.txt
   311	```
   312	
   313	**Standalone `.gz`** (not a tar) compresses a single file — there is
   314	no manifest to list. Just peek at the decompressed content:
   315	
   316	```bash
   317	zcat /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json.gz | head -50
   318	```
   319	
   320	---
   321	
   322	## EPUB / ODT
   323	
   324	```bash
   325	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/book.epub | head -200
   326	```
   327	
   328	For long ebooks, pipe through `head` — you rarely need the whole thing
   329	to answer a question.
   330	
   331	---
   332	
   333	## RTF / IPYNB
   334	
   335	```bash
   336	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notes.rtf | head -200
   337	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notebook.ipynb | head -200
   338	```
   339	
   340	---
   341	
   342	## Plain text / code / logs
   343	
   344	Check the size first:
   345	
   346	```bash
   347	wc -c /mnt/user-data/uploads/app.log
   348	```
   349	
   350	- **Under ~20KB**: `cat` is fine.
   351	- **Over ~20KB**: `head -100` and `tail -100` to orient. If the user
   352	  asked about something specific, `grep` for it. Load the whole thing
   353	  only if you genuinely need all of it.
   354	
   355	For log files, the user almost always cares about the end:
   356	
   357	```bash
   358	tail -200 /mnt/user-data/uploads/app.log
   359	```
   360	
   361	---
   362	
   363	## Unknown extension
   364	
   365	```bash
   366	file /mnt/user-data/uploads/mystery.bin
   367	xxd /mnt/user-data/uploads/mystery.bin | head -5
   368	```
   369	
   370	`file` identifies most things. `xxd` head shows magic bytes. If `file`
   371	says "data" and the hex doesn't match anything you recognize, ask the
   372	user what it is instead of guessing.
   373

ASD contains data on spectral lines with wavelengths from about 20 pm (picometers) to 60 m (meters). For many lines, ASD includes radiative transition probabilities. The energy level data include the ground states and ionization energies for ...

The Atomic Spectra Database (ASD) contains data for radiative transitions and energy levels in atoms and atomic ions. Data are included for observed transitions and energy levels of most of the known chemical elements. The links above provide access to the current lists of Holdings for Spectral Line and Energy Level Data. ASD contains data on spectral lines with wavelengths from about 20 pm (picometers) to 60 m (meters). For many lines, ASD includes radiative transition probabilities. The energy level data include the ground states and ionization energies for all spectra. Except where noted, the data have been critically evaluated by NIST. 

For most spectra, wavelengths, transition-probabilities, relative intensities, and energy levels are integrated, so that all the available information for a given transition is incorporated under a single listing.

The contents of ASD are limited to data that have been critically compiled by NIST, or, for a few spectra compiled by R.L. Kelly, published in the Journal of Physical and Chemical Reference Data for NIST. In this sense we include only NIST "Standard Reference Data." In the case of transition probabilities, for example, this means that the listed values are estimated by NIST to have the accuracy assigned to each transition. In the case of energies and wavelengths, ASD contains critically evaluated uncertainties for a large part of all data, and they are reported in the output pages. For those data that do not have an explicit information about their uncertainty, it is implied by the number of significant figures.

content.text:
The ASD Lines Search Form, referred to as the "Lines Form," provides access to transition data for atoms and ions, either in tabular or graphical form. Tabular output is available for wavelengths (or wavenumbers, or photon energies, or frequencies), relative intensities, radiative transition probabilities and related quantities, as well as energy level classifications and bibliographic references. Graphical output is available in the forms of Grotrian diagrams, line identification plots, and Saha-LTE spectrum plots. For some spectra, there is also graphical information on dependences of certain line intensity ratios on electron density and/or temperature in the emitting plasma. This information can be useful for plasma diagnostics. When loaded in the browser, the Lines Search Form displays only the Main search parameters block and the Advanced Settings block below it.



For other elements, ASD does not have both these types of energy levels and wavelengths mixed in the tables, so a prompt for this choice will not appear. The contents of the output Saha-LTE plots and tables accompanying them are explained in the corresponding Output section. The output content and features of interactive Grotrian diagrams are explained in the Plotting Grotrian diagrams section. The Grotrian Diagram can be displayed only for a spectrum of single atom or ion. Any restrictions applied to the selected data set, e.g., the wavelength/wavenumber/photon energy/frequency range, will be applied to selection of the data displayed in the diagram.

In such cases, to display narrower lines (corresponding to a lower ion temperature), the user needs to reduce the selected wavelength range, reduce the number of requested spectra, or use some line-filtering options in the Optional Search Criteria section in the Advanced Settings block of the Lines Input Form.

# 4f and 5d levels of $Ce^{3+}$ in $D_2$ eightfold oxygen coordination

Luis Seijo $^{1,2,*}$ and Zoila Barandiarán $^{1,2}$ 

<sup>1</sup>Departamento de Química, Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, 28049 Madrid, Spain <sup>2</sup>Instituto Universitario de Ciencia de Materiales Nicolás Cabrera, Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, 28049 Madrid, Spain

(Dated: June 21, 2018)

## Abstract

The effects on the 4f and 5d levels of $\mathrm{Ce}^{3+}$ of its first coordination shell geometry in Ce-doped oxides with a $D_2$ 8-fold site, like garnets, are studied with embedded cluster, wave function based ab initio methods. The only deformations of a $\mathrm{CeO}_8$ cube that are found to shift the lowest $4f \to 5d$ transition to the red are the symmetric Ce-O bond compression and the tetragonal symmetric bond bending. These results are analyzed in terms of centroid and ligand field stabilization energy differences. The splittings of the upper 5d levels and of the 4f levels are also discussed.



The energies of the 4f and 5d levels of $Ce^{3+}$ in particular garnets and in other oxides depend on the bonding and electrostatic interactions between Ce and the hosts, and they can be calculated in a one-by-one basis, with reasonable accuracy, by means of *ab initio* methods, both in $D_2$ local symmetry like in Ce-doped YAG<sup>8</sup> and in lower local symmetries like in Ce,La-doped YAG<sup>9</sup> and Ce,Ga-doped YAG.<sup>10</sup> These energies are dominated, up to first-order, by the bonding interactions between Ce and its first oxygen coordination shell, subject to the basic confinement embedding effects of the host. Other specific host embedding effects are important at higher orders of approximation and they refine the results.

This paper is aimed at providing a basic study of the energies of the levels of the $4f^1$ and $5d^1$ manifolds of Ce<sup>3+</sup> in $D_2$ 8-fold oxygen coordination.

Abstract

*Aims.* We present extensive energy level and transition data for the Ce IV spectrum. By providing accurate atomic data, we evaluate the impact of atomic data on the opacity in the neutron star merger ejecta.

*Methods.* We performed energy spectra and transition data calculations using the GRASP2018 package, which is based on the multiconfiguration Dirac–Hartree–Fock and relativistic configuration interaction methods, and the HULLAC code, which is based on a parametric potential method.

*Results.* We present energy spectra calculated for the 225 levels for the Ce3+ ion. Energy levels are compared with recommended values from the NIST Atomic Spectra Database and other available works. The root-mean-square (rms) deviations obtained for the GRASP2018 energy levels of the 5p6nl configurations from the NIST data are 1270 cm−1. The rms deviations for the HULLAC results from the NIST data are 5780 cm−1. Furthermore, electric dipole (E1) transition data, line strengths, weighted oscillator strengths, and transition rates are computed between the above levels. The computed transition rates are compared with other theoretical computations. We also evaluate the accuracy of the wave functions and transition parameters by analyzing the dependencies of the line strength *S* on the gauge parameter *G*. The gauge dependency method also allows us to determine the transitions for which the ratio between the Babushkin and Coulomb gauges shows real agreement between forms and the transitions for which the agreement between both gauges is random. Using the GRASP2018 and HULLAC data, the opacities in the neutron star merger ejecta are also calculated. We find that the opacity of Ce IV is higher than that presented by previous works, which is because of the higher completeness of our atomic data. Although the differences in the energy levels and transition probabilities cause different features in the opacity spectrum, the *Planck* mean opacities of both data sets agree within 20%.

## 1 Introduction

Observations of gravitational waves (GWs) from the neutron star (NS) merger GW170817 ([Abbott et al. 2017a](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R1)) and its electromagnetic counterpart (AT2017gfo, [Abbott et al. 2017b](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R2)) paved the way for a new method with which to study the origin of heavy elements in the Universe. The observed properties of AT2017gfo at ultraviolet, optical, and infrared wavelengths are found to be consistent with theoretically expected “kilonova”, that is, thermal emission powered by radioactive decay of newly synthesized *r*-process elements (e.g., [Li & Paczyński 1998](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R29); [Metzger et al. 2010](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R30)). This agreement indicates that *r*-process synthesis takes place in the NS merger.

Atomic data for heavy elements can be used to interpret the observed properties of kilonovae. For example, the spectra of AT2017gfo show various broad features (e.g., [Chornock et al. 2017](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R7); [Pian et al. 2017](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R31); [Smartt et al. 2017](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R36)), which are imprints of heavy elements synthesized by the NS merger. However, the elemental species have not yet been identified, except for Sr ([Watson et al. 2019](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R42); [Domoto et al. 2021](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R9)). To firmly identify the heavy elements in kilonova spectra, accurate atomic data for selected, dominant transitions are necessary.

In addition, complete atomic data are also important for understanding the nucleosynthesis in the NS merger. This is because, complete atomic data are necessary to calculate the opacity in the ejecta, which in turn determines the peak luminosity and the peak timescale of the kilonova. In particular, the presence of the lanthanide elements plays an important role in shaping the light curve of a kilonova. This is because these elements have many transitions at infrared wavelengths due to the small energy spacing, which redistribute the emission from optical to near-infrared wavelengths, making the color of the kilonova redder (the physics of the formation of emission spectra of kilonovae, in particular the role of lanthanide elements, is explained in [Kasen et al. 2013](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R24); [Barnes & Kasen 2013](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R4); [Tanaka & Hotokezaka 2013](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R37)). This property was indeed used to identify GW170817/AT2017gfo as a kilonova (e.g, [Chornock et al. 2017](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R7); [Drout et al. 2017](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R10); [Kasliwal et al. 2017](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R26); [Pian et al. 2017](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R31); [Smartt et al. 2017](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R36); [Tanvir et al. 2017](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R40); [Utsumi et al. 2017](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R41)).

To better understand the link between the emission properties of a kilonova and the nucleosynthesis therein, it is important to establish the atomic opacities of heavy elements, which requires complete atomic data (i.e., energy levels up to the excited levels and transition probabilities to the excited levels). As it is difficult to experimentally derive the complete data of energy levels and transitions, past works relied on atomic structure calculations ([Kasen et al. 2013](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R24), [2017](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R25); [Tanaka et al. 2018](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R38), [2020](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R39); [Fontes et al. 2020](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R14); [Banerjee et al. 2020](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R3)). However, in such complete atomic calculations, including excited levels, the accuracy is typically low: ~ (10–20)% in the energy levels. As a result, there is a systematic uncertainty of a factor of about 2 in the opacity ([Tanaka et al. 2018](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R38)). To further reduce the uncertainty in the opacity, more complete and accurate atomic calculations are necessary.

In this paper, we perform ab initio atomic calculations for triply ionized Ce (Ce IV) and provide an extensive evaluation of the atomic data. We choose Ce3+ because it isone of the simplest lanthanide ions with a 4f electron in the ground configuration, and is therefore an ideal ion as a benchmark of atomic calculations for complicated lanthanide elements.

The atomic structure and transitions of Ce IV have been studied by several authors. [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32) measured the lines – most of which arise from inner-shell-excited configurations – and determined 112 energy levels. [Zhang et al. (2001)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R43) measured the lifetimes for two excited levels (of the 5p6 5d configuration) of Ce IV using the time-resolved laser-induced fluorescence technique. [Savukov et al. (2003)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R35) calculated energies and transition rates for low-energy levels of Ce IV (and Pr V) using relativistic many-body perturbation theory. [Safronova et al. (2015)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R34) used a configuration interaction approach with second-order perturbation theory and a linearized coupled-cluster all-order method to compute excitation energies of Ce IV along with other ions of Ce. [Zilitis (2014)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R44) calculated oscillator strengths and lifetimes of the cesium isoelectronic sequence using the Dirac–Fock method. Recently, [Carvajal Gallego et al. (2021)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R6) used the relativistic multiconfiguration Dirac-Hartree–Fock to compute energy spectra and radiative transition data for Ce IV, as well as Ce II and Ce III.

In the present work, we performed energy spectra computations using GRASP2018 ([Froese Fischer et al. 2019](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R16)) and HULLAC (Hebrew University Lawrence Livermore Atomic Code; [Bar-Shalom et al. 2001](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R5)) codes for the 148 energy levels of the even 5p6 5d, 5p6 6s, 5p5 4f5d, 5p6 6d, 5p6 7s, 5p5 4f6s, 5p6 7d, 5p6 8s, 5p6 5g configurations and for the 77 levels of the odd 5p64f, 5p6 6p, 5p5 4f2, 5p6 5f, 5p6 7p configurations. Furthermore, we computed electric dipole (E1) transition data between these levels.

## 2 Computational procedure and scheme

### 2.1 GRASP2018 computations

The GRASP2018 package used for the computations is based on the multiconfiguration Dirac–Hartree–Fock (MCDHF) and relativistic configuration interaction (RCI) methods. In the MCDHF approximation, atomic state functions (ASFs) are given as linear combinations of symmetry adapted configuration state functions (CSFs),<!-- MathML: <math display="block" id="mml_eq1"><mrow><mo>Ψ</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>γ</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>J</mi><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext> </mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext> </mtext><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mtext> </mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext> </mtext><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mtext>CSFs</mtext></mrow></msub></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>Φ</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>P</mi><mi>J</mi><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> --> Ψ(γPJM) = ∑i = 1NCSFsciΦ(γiPJM),![Mathematical equation: \begin{equation*}\Psi({\mathit \gamma} PJM) \,{=}\, \sum_{i\,{=}\,1}^{N_{\textrm{CSFs}}} c_{i} \Phi(\gamma_{i}PJM), \end{equation*}](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21-eq1.png)(1)

where *J* and *M* are the angular quantum numbers, *P* is parity, *N*CSFs is the number of CSFs, *c**i* are signed amplitudes of CSF contributions, and *γ* contains all additional quantum numbers required to uniquely characterize a CSF. The CSFs Φ(*γ**i* *PJM*) are built from products of one-electron Dirac orbitals. In the relativistic self-consistent field procedure, both the radial parts of the Dirac orbitals and the expansion coefficients were optimized to self-consistency.

In RCI computations, the atomic state function is expanded in CSFs, and only the expansion coefficients are determined by diagonalizing the Hamiltonian matrix. The RCI method was used to include the transverse-photon (Breit) interaction and the quantum electrodynamic (QED) corrections: vacuum polarization and self-energy. More details about MCHDF and RCI methods can be found in [Froese Fischer et al. (2016)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R15) and [Grant (2007)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R22).

In this work, ASFs were obtained as expansions over *jj*-coupled CSFs. To transform these ASFs into an *LSJ*-coupled CSF basis for labeling purposes, the method provided by [Gaigalas et al. (2003](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R17), [2017](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R19)) was used.

Generation of the initial wave functions begins from the MCDHF computation of the ground [Xe]4f configuration. These orbitals were kept frozen and used in further computations. In the next step, the 5d, 5f, 5g, 6s, 6p, 6d, 7s, 7p, 7d, 8s orbitals belonging to the configurations of the multireference (MR) set were optimized (these computations are referred to as MR below). The MR set consists of the 5p65d, 5p6 6s, 5p5 4f5d, 5p6 6d, 5p6 7s, 5p5 4f6s, 5p6 7d, 5p6 8s, 5p6 5g even and 5p64f, 5p6 6p, 5p5 4f2, 5p6 5f, 5p6 7p odd configurations. A similar technique for generation of the initial wave functions was already applied to Nd ions ([Gaigalas et al. 2019](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R20)) and Er III ([Gaigalas et al. 2020](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R21)).

Unless stated otherwise, the inactive core used in the present calculations is [Kr]4d105s2. The even and odd states were optimized separately. In the following steps of the MCDHF computation, active spaces (AS) of CSFs were generated by allowing single (S) substitutions from the 5p shell to {8s, 7p, 7d, 5f, 5g} orbitals and single-double (SD) substitutions from the 4f, 5d, 5f, 5g, 6s, 6p, 6d, 7s, 7p, 7d, 8s shells to the orbital spaces (OS): OS1 = {9s, 8p, 8d, 6f, 6g}, OS2 = {10s, 9p, 9d, 7f, 7g, 6h}, and OS3 = {11s,10p,10d,8f,8g,7h}. Thus, valence-valence (VV) electron correlations were included in the computations. When a new OS is being computed, the previous orbitals are frozen. The MCDHF calculations were performed in the extended optimal level (EOL) scheme ([Dyall et al. 1989](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R11)). [Table 1](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#T1) summarizes the calculations performed for even and odd configurations by showing their *J* and parity values and the ASFs that were included in the optimization process. Based on the orbitals from the MCDHF calculations, further RCI calculations were performed, including calculation of the Breit interaction and leading QED effects. By analyzing the mean radii of the orbitals, we find that the 4f orbitals are closer to the other *n* = 4 orbitals than either 5s or 5p. Therefore, the 5s orbital is considered to be valence as well. Further on, the 5s closed shell was opened for S substitutions to the {8s, 7p, 7d, 5f, 5g} orbitals in the RCI computations (VV2 strategy) to include additional correlation effects. In the last step, the MR set was extended to include additional important configurations based on the analysis of ASFs composition. In final computations, single-restricted-double (SrD) substitutions (allowing double (D) substitutions only from different shells) to the {8s, 7p, 7d, 5f, 5g} orbitals were added in the active space (VV3 strategy). The inclusion of electron correlation allowing substitutions from the 5s shell and the extension of the MR set increase the AS very rapidly, and so limitations on substitutions were applied.

### 2.2 HULLAC computations

HULLAC is a coherent set of programs that calculates the atomic structure and rates of radiative and collisional processes ([Bar-Shalom et al. 2001](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R5)). HULLAC uses fully relativistic orbitals to calculate the energy levels and radiative transition probabilities. The atomic relativistic states are obtained from the many-electron Hamiltonian<!-- MathML: <math display="block" id="mml_eq2"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mtext> </mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext> </mtext><mi>H</mi><mtext>{'}</mtext><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mtext>Breit</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mtext>QED</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> --> H = H{'}+HBreit+HQED,![Mathematical equation: \begin{equation*} H \,{=}\, H{\prime} + H_{\textrm{Breit}} + H_{\textrm{QED}}, \end{equation*}](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21-eq2.png)(2)

where H′ is the Dirac–Coulomb Hamiltonian, and *H*Breit and *H*QED are the Breit interaction and QED correction used as the second-order perturbation.

The single electron orbital wavefunction is obtained by solving the Dirac equation for an effective central field potential. The effective potential is obtained by solving the Poisson equation for a nuclear point charge *Zδ*(*r*) and the electron charge distribution ([Bar-Shalom et al. 2001](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R5))<!-- MathML: <math display="block" id="mml_eq3"><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext> </mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext> </mtext><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>q</mi><mi>N</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>exp</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> --> ρ(r) = −4πr2qN[rl+1exp(−αr/2)]2,![Mathematical equation: \begin{equation*} \rho(r) \,{=}\, {-}4\pi r^{2} q N [r^{l+1}\textrm{exp}(-\alpha r/2)]^{2},\end{equation*}](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21-eq3.png)(3)

with the boundary condition that at *r* = *∞*, the potential converges to (*Z* − *q*)∕*r*. Here, *N* is the normalization operator, *q* is the number of electrons, and *α* is the free parameter representing the average radius of the Slater type orbital. The free parameter *α* is obtained by minimization of the first-order configuration-average energies. For our calculation of Ce IV, the central potential as seen by the last electron is determined by removing one electron from the ground configuration 5p6 4f ([Kramida et al. 2020](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R27)), which gives 5p6. The potential is also optimized for the ground configuration. We note that the energy levels for Ce IV are calculated for all the configurations of the MR set mentioned in Sect. [2.1](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#S3), including the ground state.

The *N*-electron zero-order solution or the configuration state function (CSF) are derived as the anti-symmetrized product of the single-electron zero-order solution of the orbitals in the chosen coupling scheme (*jj* in this case). A Hamiltonian matrix, including the Breit interaction and the leading QED correction of multi-CSFs, is diagonalized as in the RCI method of GRASP2018. As a result, ASFs are obtained as linear combinations of the CSFs.

## 3 Results

### 3.1 Evaluation of energy spectra

In this work, excitation energies were computed for the 148 states of the even 5p6 5d, 5p6 6s, 5p5 4f5d, 5p6 6d, 5p6 7s, 5p5 4f6s, 5p6 7d, 5p6 8s, and 5p6 5g configurations and for the 77 statesof the odd 5p64f, 5p6 6p, 5p5 4f2, 5p6 5f, and 5p6 7p configurations using the GRASP2018 and HULLAC codes. [Table A.1](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#T7) displays energy spectra and the atomic state function composition in *LS*-coupling from the GRASP2018 calculations for levels of these configurations. The levels are given with unique labels ([Gaigalas et al. 2017](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R19)). In the computed spectra there are levels, for which the assigned labels are not based on the largest contribution to the composition. These are marked in bold font in [Table A.1](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#T7). Energy levels were computed up to the 31 eV energy limit.

The Atomic Spectra Database (ASD) of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST; [Kramida et al. 2020](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R27)) provides only 16 energy levels of the 5p6nl configurations for the Ce IV spectrum; these are based on [Lang (1936)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R28). [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32) presented 112 experimental energy levels, most of them belonging to the inner-shell-excited configurations (5p5 4f5d and 5p5 4f6s). Energy levels given by [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32) fully agree with the values given in the NIST ASD ([Kramida et al. 2020](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R27)) except energies for the 5p6 7d 2D5∕2 and 5p6 5g 2G7∕2,9∕2 states. [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32) found the [Lang (1936)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R28) 5g, 7d5∕2, and 8s levels to be spurious and determined new values for the 5p6 7d 2D5∕2 state and for the states of the 5p65g configuration.

To evaluate the accuracy of the results, the calculated energy levels were compared with data from the NIST ASD ([Kramida et al. 2020](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R27)) and experimental or other theoretical results. The comparison of computed (with GRASP2018 and HULLAC codes) energy levels and experimental ([Reader & Wyart 2009](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32)) or theoretical ones ([Savukov et al. 2003](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R35) and [Safronova et al. 2015](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R34)) with the NIST ASD, giving a difference (in cm−1) Δ*E* = *E*NIST − *E*calc, is presentedin [Table 2](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#T2). The NIST ASD specifies one energy value (225 625 cm−1) for the two unresolved levels of the 5p65g configuration. When comparing this energy level with other works, the level with the lower energy was compared. In the case of [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32) and GRASP2018 results, the lower energy belongs to the level with *J* = 7∕2, while in the case of HULLAC, the lower level has *J* = 9∕2. As we can see from the table, computed energies of GRASP2018 agree well with recommended values from the NIST ASD. The root-mean-square (rms) deviations obtained for energy levels of the 5p6 nl configurations from the NIST data are 1270 cm−1. The HULLAC energy levels in comparison with the NIST data are too high, and the rms deviations from the NIST data are 5780 cm−1. When comparing the results of other theoretical investigations ([Savukov et al. 2003](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R35) and [Safronova et al. 2015](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R34)) with the NIST ASD, the rms deviations are 2160 cm−1 and 2240 cm−1, respectively;but those authors only investigated low-lying levels.

It should be mentioned that the order of the levels of the 5p6 6d 2D term in the GRASP2018 results disagrees with the NIST ASD. Considering the order of these states in HULLAC studies and in the calculations performed by [Savukov et al. (2003)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R35), it is seen that the order agreeswith the NIST ASD, but the splitting is much smaller. In the HULLAC case, it is only 15 cm−1, in [Savukov et al. (2003)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R35) it is 720 cm−1, while in the NIST ASD this splitting reaches 1715 cm−1. [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32) show that this anomalous fine structure is the result of interaction between 5p6 6d and the inner-shell excited configuration 5p54f5d. Whereas there is good agreement between GRASP2018 and NIST data for most energy levels, and the order for other levels is correct, a deeper analysis was performed for the levels of the 5p6 6d 2D term to clarify this disagreement. In [Fig. 1](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F1), the convergence of these levels by including different correlations is presented. As seen from the figure, in the MR computations, the 5p 6 6d 2D3∕2 level is lower than 5p66d 2D5∕2. By including the correlations (VV2), the order of the levels is inverted and does not change by extending the orbital space. It was shown that the energy values converge to the NIST results by extending the orbital space from OS1 to OS3 (in the VV2 strategy), and the energies are very close to the NIST recommended values at OS3. By including the additional correlations (VV3 strategy; see OS3* in [Fig. 1](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F1)), the order of the states is inverted and the 2D3∕2 level becomes the lower one. The figure also shows that the Breit and QED corrections have little influence on the energies. In [Fig. 1](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F1), HULLAC results are also presented. HULLAC energy levels can be seen to be higher than energies given in the NIST ASD, and as the splitting between the fine-structure levels is very small, results for the two levels overlap.

We also analyzed the composition of these levels present our findings in [Fig. 2](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F2) and [Table 3](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#T3). In [Fig. 2](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F2) only the main contributors from different strategies are presented, while [Table 3](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#T3) shows the total contribution of each configuration to these two levels when different strategies are applied. After including correlations with the VV3 strategy, the weight of the 5p6 6d configuration decreases in the 5p66d 2D3∕2 level, and the influence of the 5p54f5d configuration increases. For the 5p66d 2D5∕2 state, the situation is vice versa. From [Fig. 2](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F2) it is seen that the 5p66d 2D3∕2 state is quite pure in the HULLAC computations (about 88%), while in the final GRASP2018 results the 5p66d contributionis smaller; it constitutes 58% in the composition and is close to that found by [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32). The 5p66d 2D5∕2 state is purer (about 80%) in the final GRASP2018 calculations, while in the HULLAC and [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32) investigations, it is 48% and 50%, respectively. From the analysis, it is seen that the change in the order of the two states in the final results is affected by the MR set extension and inclusion of additional correlations in the VV3 strategy. To study the accuracy of the GRASP2018 results, we also analyzed the convergence for the levels with the same orbital angular momenta (*l* = 3) but with higher principal quantum number (*n* = 7). [Figure 3](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F3) presents the convergence of the 5p6 7d2D term states when different correlations are included. Energy levels of the 5p67d configuration in the final results agree very well with NIST data. The fine-structure levels of the 5p67d 2D term have the same trends as those of the 5p66d 2D term. The 2D3∕2 and 2D5∕2 levels are inverted when the VV2 strategy is used, and the order of the states changes when correlations are added with the VV3 strategy. The accuracy of the results and the quality of the wave functions of the 5p66d 2D term are analyzed in Sect. [3.2](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#S7).

[Figures 4](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F4) and [5](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F5) present the comparison of computed (with the GRASP2018 and HULLAC codes) energy levels with energy levels given by [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32). The HULLAC and GRASP2018 energy levels were related by comparing the compositions in *jj* coupling with the data of [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32). [Figures 4](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F4) and [5](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F5) show three distinct groups of energy levels. As seen from [Fig. 4](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F4), the agreement with GRASP2018 for the levels of the 5p54fnl configurations is poorer than it is for the 5p6nl configurations, the difference reaches 16 000 cm−1 for some levels. The HULLAC results (see [Fig. 5](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F5)) are in good agreement with those of [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32) for the levels of the 5p54f5d and 5p54f6s configurations. The rms deviations for energy spectra of these configurations from the [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32) data are displayed in [Table 4](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#T4).

### 3.2 Evaluation of transition data

The accuracy of the wave functions and the uncertainties of the transition parameters were evaluated by: (1) analyzing the dependence of the line strength *S* on the gauge parameter *G* ([Rudzikas 2007](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R33)); (2) analyzing the dependence of the cancelation factor (CF; [Cowan 1981](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R8)) on the gauge parameter *G*; (3) studying the *dT* parameter defined in [Ekman et al. (2014)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R13), which shows the relative difference between the Babushkin and Coulomb gauges of the computed transition rates; (4) comparing the computed transition data with other available data. For this purpose transitions from different regions of energy spectra were chosen as illustrated in [Fig. 6](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F6). The dependencies of the line strengths on the gauge parameter *G* for the studied transitions are displayed in [Figs. 7](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F7)–[13](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F13). Here, the lines strengths from the present HULLAC computations and from other works are also plotted. As seen from the figures, the correlations included in the final computations (the VV3 strategy) are very important for all studied transitions and especially for transitions between highly excited levels or from highly excited levels to the ground configuration ([Figs. 9](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F9)–[13](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F13)). In [Figs. 7](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F7)–[8](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F8), the gauge dependence changes monotonically upon increasing the orbital spaces or upon including additional correlations. For the studied transitions, the dependence is closer to linear when correlations included in the final computations (the VV3 strategy) are added. Also, the minimum position of the parabola (the *G**S* = 0 values) – which shows the accuracy of the wave functions – for the VV3 strategy is larger than for other strategies. Thus, the wave functions of the final results should be more accurate than from the VV2 strategy. The *dT* parameter for the studied transitions was poorer for all choices of *OS* of the VV2 strategy than in the final results. The *G**S* = 0 values together with the *dT* parameters of the VV3 strategy are presented in [Table 5](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#T5). The magnitude of *dT* is smaller for transitions that have more accurate wave functions. The minimum position of the parabola is also important for predicting how the results will change by improving the calculations. If the Babushkin and Coulomb gauges are close to the minimum position of the parabola, then improving the computations will not significantly change the results. If the Babushkin and Coulomb gauges are on the parabola, then improvement of the computations will lead to a relatively large change in the results.

In this section, we present the results of an evaluation of the quality of the wave functions for the 5p66d 2D3∕2 and 5p66d 2D5∕2 levels whichwas carried out because a disagreement was found in the order of these levels as compared with the NIST data. To this end, we analyzed the transitions in which the 5p66d 2D term participates, and the dependence of the line strength *S* on the gauge parameter *G* is presented in [Figs. 12](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F12)–[13](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F13). By analyzing the gauge dependence, we see that the wave functions of the 5p66d 2D levels in the final computations (the VV3 strategy) are more accurate than they are in other strategies. From the analysis, it follows that the final results (the VV3 strategy, with the 5p66d 2D3∕2 level lower than 5p66d 2D5∕2) are more accurate than results from other strategies.

Further, to determine which gauge parameter *G* is more suitable, we studied the cancelation factor (CF; [Cowan 1981](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R8) The dependencies of the CF on the gauge parameter *G* for the studied transitions are shown in [Figs. 14](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F14)–[20](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F20). [Table A.2](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#T11) presents a comparison of the computed wavelengths and transition probabilities with results from [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32), [Carvajal Gallego et al. (2021)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R6), and [Savukov et al. (2003)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R35). The rms of the relative differences of the GRASP2018 results from the experimental wavelengths ([Reader & Wyart 2009](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32)) is about 2%, 11%, and 19% for transitions between 5p6nl − 5p6nl, 5p6nl − 5p54fnl, and 5p6nl−HE, respectively.[Carvajal Gallego et al. (2021)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R6) presented transition rates for 37 lines of Ce IV. However, these authors do not give the energy spectra in their paper for this ion. Therefore, only transitions for which the energy levels could be related with the NIST energies have been compared here.

[Figure 21](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F21) presents a comparison of the computed line strengths from the present work and other theoretical calculations ([Carvajal Gallego et al. 2021](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R6); [Savukov et al. 2003](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R35)) with results from [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32). The agreement between all theoretical methods is similar, except for three transitions from 5p65d to the ground configuration, for which all other calculations do not agree with the results from [Savukov et al. (2003)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R35). The best agreement with results from [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32) was achieved for transitions (with *S* >1), where the rms deviations for all theoretical methods are about (11–15)%. It should be mentioned that all transitions presented in [Fig. 21](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F21) are between levels of the 5p6nl configurations. [Figure 22](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F22) presents a comparison of the computed line strengths from GRASP2018 with results of [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32), where transitions between different groups of configurations are distinguished. The agreement between both results and the deviations within the same line strength range differ for transitions from different groups. This is especially notable for transitions with greater line strength. [Figure 23](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F23) presents a comparison of transitions of the 5p6nl group between the results from two GRASP2018 strategies and the results from [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32). Here, most of the results are in better agreement with the VV2 strategy, which by the analysis presented above was evaluated as less accurate than the VV3 strategy.

Usually, calculated transition rates are more accurate for greater line strengths than for weaker ones. By analyzing the agreement of the line strength of the final GRASP2018 results between both forms, it was observed that ratios of the two forms have different distributions within the same range of line strengths, depending on the configurations involved. Some of the computed GRASP2018 transitions are presented in [Fig. 24](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F24), where transitions between different groups of configurations are distinguished. Deviations of line strengths for the transitions from different groups differ within the same line strength range. This is also seen in [Fig. 22](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F22), where the results from the present study are compared with those of [Reader & Wyart (2009)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R32). This means that not all levels are described with equal accuracy, even levels from the same configuration group. When a large number of levels is computed, and the highest levels are close to the ionization limit, it is quite difficult to achieve the same accuracy for all computed levels. The goal of this work is to compute as many levels as possible, taking into account the complexity of the task and limitation of computer resources. Therefore, 225 energy levels were computed up to the 31 eV energy limit, which is close to the ionization energy (36.906 eV). Also, all possible transitions were calculated between these levels. From the above analysis, it follows that the accuracy of the transitions with similar line strengths should likely be different. Here, transitions were plotted against the *G**S* = 0 parameter, which helps to identify the most accurate transitions.

The distribution of line strength *S* as a function of *G**S* = 0 parameter is presented in [Fig. 25](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F25). From the gauge dependence analysis, which shows the quality of the wave functions ([Rudzikas 2007](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R33)), it follows that the most accurate results have greater *G**S* = 0. [Figure 25](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F25) shows that the most accurate results are in different ranges of line strengths. For example, if the *G**S* = 0 parameter is fixed at a value of 100, the values of the line strength *S* vary in the range of (0.0001–20) a.u. Also, the line strengths of similar magnitude have different accuracy. For example, if the range of *S* = (0.01–0.1) a.u. is fixed, the *G**S* = 0 parameter varies in the range (0.01–6000). Therefore, if transitions with similar line strengths are evaluated together, the accuracy will be overestimated or underestimated for some of them, depending on the *G**S* = 0 parameter.

Taking all of the above into account, the uncertainties of the final GRASP2018 transition data were estimated based on quantitative and qualitative evaluation of the transition parameters. [Figure 26](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F26) shows the connection between quantitative (natural logarithm of the ratio of line strength *S* in the Babushkin form to the line strength *S* in the Coulomb form) and qualitative (gauge dependence analysis) evaluation of the transition data. [Figure 26](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F26) can be divided into three parts: (1) the upper part of the graph (blue points), where − *∞* < *G**S* = 0 < 0; (2) the lower left part of the graph (red points), where <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" id="mml_eq44"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo><</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mtext> </mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext> </mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo><</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></mrow></math> --> 0<GS = 0<2![Mathematical equation: $0 < G_{S\,{=}\,0} < \sqrt{2}$](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21-eq26.png); and (3) the lower right part of the graph (green points), where <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" id="mml_eq45"><mrow><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mo><</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mtext> </mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext> </mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo><</mo><mi>∞</mi></mrow></math> --> 2<GS = 0<∞![Mathematical equation: $\sqrt{2} < G_{S\,{=}\,0} < \infty$](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21-eq27.png). In the case where *G**S* = 0 is in the range between the Coulomb and Babushkin gauges (the lower left part of [Fig. 26](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F26)), the values of the transition parameter in the two forms are on different branches of the parabola represented by Eq. ([4](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#FD4)). In this case, the agreement between both gauges is random, and cannot be used as the accuracy indicator. In two other cases, when the value of *G**S* = 0 is smaller than zero or greater than <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" id="mml_eq46"><mrow><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></mrow></math> --> 2![Mathematical equation: $\sqrt{2}$](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21-eq28.png), the values in the Coulomb and Babushkin gauges are on the same branch of the parabola of Eq. ([4](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#FD4)), the ratio between the two shows real agreement and can be used for accuracy estimation. Therefore, only transitions belonging to the ranges with − *∞* < *G**S* = 0 < 0 or <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" id="mml_eq47"><mrow><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mo><</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mtext> </mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext> </mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo><</mo><mi>∞</mi></mrow></math> --> 2<GS = 0<∞![Mathematical equation: $\sqrt{2} < G_{S\,{=}\,0} < \infty$](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21-eq29.png) can be evaluated based on the ratio between the two gauges. The computed transition strengths from these two groups were divided into groups according to the natural logarithm of the ratio (see [Fig. 27](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F27)). Transitions with similar agreement between the two gauges (or with similar *G**S* = 0 parameter) were assigned to the same accuracy class. The limits of the accuracy classes were chosen according to the NIST ASD ([Kramida et al. 2020](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R27)) terminology (AA ≤ 1%, A+ ≤ 2%, A ≤ 3%, B+ ≤ 7%, B ≤ 10%, C+ ≤ 18%, C ≤ 25%, D+ ≤ 40%, D ≤ 50%, and E > 50%). All the remaining transitions with <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" id="mml_eq48"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo><</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mtext> </mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext> </mtext><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo><</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></mrow></math> --> 0<GS = 0<2![Mathematical equation: $0 < G_{S\,{=}\,0} < \sqrt{2}$](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21-eq30.png) were not evaluated, and were assigned to the accuracy class E.

To evaluate the total uncertainties of *A* and *gf* values, the uncertainties of the transition energy should be added. Transition energy uncertainties should be scaled by a factor of 3 for *A* or by factor of 1 for *gf*, because *A* is proportional to the cube of transitionenergy Δ*E*, while *gf* is proportional to the first power of Δ*E*.

The transition data from the GRASP2018 calculations, such as wavelengths, weighted oscillator strengths, line strengths, and transition rates of E1 transitions, are given in Table 6 along with the *dT* parameter, the *G**S* = 0 parameter, and the estimated accuracy. The full table is available at the CDS.

The computed lifetimes for some levels are compared with experimental values and other theoretical calculations in [Table 7](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#T6). The GRASP2018 lifetimes of the 5p66d 2D are lower than the experimental values by 18% and 23% for 2D3∕2 and 2D5∕2, respectively.These lifetimes were recalculated using the experimental wavelengths for the radiative transition probabilities. This way, the errors stemming from uncertainties of the transition energies were eliminated, while the uncertainties coming from calculations of the line strength were estimated using the relative difference (*τ**B* − *τ**C*)∕min(*τ**B*, *τ**C*) (Col. 1(adj.) in [Table 7](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#T6)). Recalculated GRASP2018 lifetimes of the 5p66d 2D decreased a little, and the estimated uncertainty of calculations for these levels is about 29%. The HULLAC lifetimes for these levels are too low by 33% and 37% for 2D3∕2 and 2D5∕2, respectively.The lifetimes calculated by [Savukov et al. (2003)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#R35) are almost three times lower than the experimental ones. The lifetimes of the 5p66p 2P levels in GRASP2018 have an uncertainty of about 3%, and they are in good agreement with other theoretical results.

[Figures 28](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F28) and [29](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/02/aa41513-21/aa41513-21.html#F29) show the statistical evaluation of oscillator strengths and wavelengths of E1 transitions from the GRASP2018 and HULLAC computations. GRASP2018 gives more transitions in the range of log(*gf*) < −3, while HULLAC gives more transitions with log(*gf*) > −3. The largest difference between the GRASP2018 and HULLAC results is in the range of log(*gf*) = (−3.4 to −3.2). In the statistical distribution of the wavelengths, the difference between GRASP2018 and HULLAC results is not very large.

content.title: 4f fine-structure levels as the dominant error in the electronic   structures of binary lanthanide oxides
content.text:
Based on band theory, the 4f fine levels are assigned variously below, above and within the 2p-5d optical transition gap in lanthanide oxides across the periodic table from La to Lu.

Elucidation of the electronic properties of these materials using theoretical methods is challenging because most of these materials are mixed valence or heavy fermion systems. <sup>4,5</sup> In addition to exhibiting strong correlation, the f-electrons also couple with the s, p, and d (mainly 5d) electrons. This imposes stringent requirements for an accurate description of the electronic states. In this work, to treat the electronic structures of f-electron solids using a simpler model, we focus on the relative energy differences between the 4f energy levels and the occupied valence band maximum (VBM), which is one of the possible sources of error in density functional theory (DFT) electronic structure calculations for 4f- or 5f-based solids.
