content.text:
Singly ionised iron (Fe II, Z=26) is one of the main species of interest. Reference spectral line data for astrophysical spectral synthesis are never complete and always subject to improvement. For Fe II, the current challenge arises from closely packed highly excited energy levels near the ionisation limit (e.g. levels of the $3d^64f$ and $3d^65d$ configurations, referred to as the 4f and 5d levels), requiring observation of the Fe II spectrum under a variety of plasma conditions and extensive parameterisation of semi-empirical atomic structure calculations (e.g. Kurucz 2017; Cowan 1981).

Castelli & Kurucz (2010) had identified 109 4f and 14 (4, 5, and 6)d energy levels of Fe II using only high-resolution spectra of the Fe-overabundant chemically peculiar star HR 6000 recorded by the UVES instrument at the VLT. 

Soon after, the most extensive and recent laboratory investigation of the spectrum and energy levels of Fe II by Nave & Johansson (2012) confirmed roughly half of the levels identified by Castelli & Kurucz (2010).

In this paper, we present identification of 24 energy levels of the 4f and 5d singly excited configurations of Fe II that were proposed by analysing stellar spectra (Castelli & Kurucz 2010) but were unable to be confirmed by laboratory spectroscopy of Fe II by Nave & Johansson (2012). In total, 125 transitions within 5072 – 7868 Å were observed and classified in the identification of these 24 levels, with

Milan Ding, 1\* Hiroki Kozuki, 1 Florence Concepcion, 1 Gillian Nave2 and Juliet C. Pickering1

<sup>1</sup>Blackett Laboratory, Imperial College London, London SW7 2AZ, UK

Accepted XXX. Received YYY; in original form ZZZ

# ABSTRACT

Many energy levels of singly ionised iron (Fe II, Z = 26) remain uncertain or experimentally unknown. Their identification and spectral line data are required in reliable astrophysical spectral analyses. In motivation for improving the atomic data of Fe II, we analysed emission spectra of a Fe-Ne plasma produced by a Penning discharge lamp recorded by high-resolution Fourier transform spectroscopy in the region $9000 - 27,000 \text{ cm}^{-1} (11,111 - 3704 \text{ Å})$ . content.text:
Abstract
Measurements of the spectrum of doubly ionized praseodymium from 821 to 2103 Å are given. One hundred fifty-three energy levels deduced from these wavelengths and an earlier line-list of longer wavelengths are presented. These levels are identified with the configurations 4f26s, 4f27s, 4f28s, 4f26p, 4f26d, 4f25f, 5d24f, and 4f5d6s and are given term designations. Radial energy integrals belonging to these configurations are parametrically deduced from the known levels.
A value of 21.625 eV (174420 cm−1) for the ionization energy of Pr iii, with an estimated uncertainty of 0.016 eV (130 cm−1), is derived from the 4f2ns series (n = 6, 7, 8).
Keywords: Energy levels, interaction parameters, praseodymium, third spectrum, vacuum ultraviolet, wavelengths
1. Introduction


The analysis of Pr iii in the wavelength range from 2025 to 10716 Å [1,2]1 revealed nearly completely the energy level structure of the four low-lying configurations 4f3, 4f25d, 4f26s, and 4f26p, and some levels of 5d24f and 4f26d. I have extended the observations to shorter wavelengths and measured 2948 lines in the range from 821 to 2103 Å. These new data have led to a considerable increase in the number of known levels of the 5d24f configuration and to the discovery of levels belonging to the 4f5d6s, 4f25f, and 4f28s configurations. In addition, a reexamination of the old line-list yielded more levels of the configurations 4f26s, 4f26d, and 4f27s. In all, 153 energy levels of Pr iii have been newly established.
The configurations to which they belong were treated theoretically for the purpose of determining parametrically the radial energy integrals and of calculating the level positions and eigenvectors.

Resonance lines of Cs II, Ba III, and La IVThe resonance line spectra of ions in the Xe I isoelectronic sequence, consisting of the five transitions to the 5p6 150 ground state from levels with J = 1 in the 5p5 5d and 6s configurations, have been observed for Cs II, Ba III, and La IV. The observations were made with a sliding spark on the 10.7-m normal-incidence vacuum spectrograph at NBS. The resonance transitions from the 5p5 6d and 7s configurations were also observed for these ions, except for that from 5p5 6d 3P1 of Ba III. Several resonance transitions from higher nd and ns levels were also observed. Estimated values for the J = 1 levels of the 5p5 7s configuration of Ce V were obtained by extrapolation. The derived ionization energies in eV are Cs II 23.17(4), Ba III 35.79(6), La IV 45.95(6), Ce V 65.55(25).

# The Fifth Spectrum of Praseodymium

[Victor Kaufman](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term="Kaufman%20V"[Author])

Find articles by [Victor Kaufman](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term="Kaufman%20V"[Author])

PMCID: PMC6658507 PMID: [31824068](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31824068/)

## Abstract

Twelve spectral lines of quadruply-ionized praseodymium in the region 840 to 2250 Å are reported. Five terms (4*f*2F, 5*d* 2D, 6s 2S, 6*p* 2P, and *Is* 2S) and the hyperfine splitting of the 6s 2S term are given. A calculation of the principal ionization energy (Pr4+ → Pr5+) leads to a value of 57.44 eV with an estimated uncertainty of ±0.05 eV.

**Keywords:** Atomic energy levels, isoelectronic sequence, praseodymiun, rare earth, spectrum, sliding spark discharge lamp

## 1. Introduction

The one-electron Cs I isoelectronic sequence has been observed through Ce IV. The present work extends this to Pr V. Several orbital properties such as quantum defect, doublet splitting, and term energy intervals were found to vary in a regular way through the Cs I sequence. These regularities have been used here to verify the analysis of Pr V.

This is the first example of the structure of the fifth spectrum of a rare earth. The regularities in the level structure of the 4*f* period of atoms in lower stages of ionization indicate that Pr V may serve as a guide to the interpretation of the more complex fifth spectra of the rare earths.

## 2. Experimental Procedure

The spectrum plates obtained in the investigation of Pr IV [[1](#R1)][1](#FN1) were found to contain several very strong and fairly isolated lines in a 500-A spark exposure which showed no trace in the 50-A exposure. These could only be interpreted as high excitation Pr IV lines, which is unlikely because of their unusual strength, or Pr V lines. Unfortunately, the sliding-spark light source [[2](#R2)] used in this experiment does not suppress Pr IV relative to Pr V. Therefore, the assignment of these lines to Pr V could not be based exclusively on excitation separation.

Exposures were made in the first order of a 35-ft Eagle vacuum spectrograph at a reciprocal dispersion of 0.78 Å/mm. For further corroboration of the lines of the 6*s*–6*p* and 6*p*–7*s* transitions and for a better intensity relationship between these lines, exposures were also made in the first order of a 2.2-meter Eagle vacuum spectrograph at a reciprocal dispersion of 2.75 Å/mm. Calculated and measured wavelengths of C, N, O, Si, Ge, and Cu in various stages of ionization were used as standards of calibration [[3](#R3)–[7](#R7)]. The estimated wavelength uncertainty for all lines, except those at 1958 Å, is ±0.005 Å. Those at 1958 Å have an estimated uncertainty of ±0.003 Å.

## 3. Wavelengths and Energy Levels

A list of the classified lines of Pr V, including visual estimates of their relative intensities, wavenumbers, and classifications is given in [table 1](#T1). The list of energy levels of Pr V derived therefrom is given in [table 2](#T2). It includes the level designation, the observed position with estimated uncertainty, the fine structure splitting where appropriate, and the hyperfine structure splitting for the 6*s* 2S term. The hyperfine splitting of the 7*s* level is calculated to be about 1. cm−1. Because the width of the 6*p*–7*s* lines is about 2. cm−1, this splitting could not be observed.

The interpretation of the observed spectral lines was begun with an accurate estimate of *ζ*4*f* obtained from the 4*f*6*s* configuration of Pr3+. This value allowed an unambiguous interpretation of the intense 4*f* – 5*d* lines. Using this 5*d* doublet splitting, we were able to interpret the almost-equally prominent 5*d*–6*p* lines. In [figure 1](#F1), the ratios of the spin-orbit splitting, Δ*T* to *Z**a* are plotted against *Z**a* in the Cs I isoelectronic sequence. The spin-orbit splittings are those of the 4*f*2F, 5*d*2D, and 6p2P terms, and *Z*(*l* is the positive charge on the ion remaining after the removal of the outer electron. The values for Pr V provide smooth extensions of the curves drawn through the previously known points.

### Figure 1. Variation of <!-- MathML: <math id="M1" overflow="linebreak"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>T</mtext></mrow><mrow><msub><mtext>Z</mtext><mrow><mtext>a</mtext></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> --> ΔTZa along the Cs I isoelectronic sequence where ΔT equals spin-orbit splittings of the 4f 2F, 5d 2D, and 6p 2P terms.

[![Figure 1.](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/b056/6658507/6223c41b2ebb/jres-71A-583-g001.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=6658507_jres-71A-583-g001.jpg)

*Note the anomalous position of the Ba II 4*f*2F point. References for the plotted values are Cs I; H. Kleiman, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 52, 441 (1962), Ba II; E. Rasmussen, Zeit. f. Phys. 83, 404 (1933), La III; see ref. [[10](#R10)]. Ce IV; see ref. [[8](#R8)].*

The combinations of the 6*p* 2P term with the 6*s* and 7*s* 2S levels were not so easily distinguished because of the comparable strength of numerous Pr IV lines in the same spectral region. Evidence for our interpretation of these lines in terms of the behavior of the 6*s* – 7*s* energy interval is presented in [figure 2](#F2) where the observed value for Pr V follows the smooth variation of this interval in the Cs I isoelectronic sequence.

### Figure 2. Variation of the ratio of separation of the 6s 2S and 7s 2S terms to Za along the isoelectronic sequence.

[![Figure 2.](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/b056/6658507/b8da85b1b336/jres-71A-583-g002.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=6658507_jres-71A-583-g002.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6658507/figure/F2/)

*For references for the plotted values see the caption of [figure 1](#F1).*

In [figure 3](#F3) we present the sequential behavior of the quantum defect, *n* – *n**a*, for each of the observed terms. These points are interrelated since the quantum defects depend on the positions of the terms relative to the ionization limit which in turn is determined by the positions of the *ns* 2S terms. Therefore the agreement of the Pr V experimental values with the isoelectronic sequence is a strong confirmation of the analysis of this spectrum.

### Figure 3. Variation of quantum defect of the center of gravity of the 4f, 5d, 6p, 6s, and 7s terms along the Cs I isoelectronic sequence.
![Figure 3.](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/b056/6658507/bef846c15221/jres-71A-583-g003.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6658507/figure/F3/)

*Note the anomalous position of the Ba II 4*f* point. The error bar on the 7*s* 2S Pr V point indicates the variation in the quantum defect for a change in the ionization energy of ±400 cm−1. For references for the plotted values see the caption of [figure 1](#F1).*

Because of the noticeable departure of the Ba II 4*f*2F points in [figures 1](#F1) and [3](#F3), we have examined the *nf* series of Ba II in detail and found that the behavior of (*n – n**a*) versus <!-- MathML: <math id="M14" overflow="linebreak"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> --> 1/na2 is quite different from that of the same series in Cs I and La III. It is our impression that this part of the Ba II analysis bears reexamination.

The value of the spin-orbit parameter, *ζ*4*f*, derived from the 4*f*2*F* term of Pr V equals 865.0±0.3 cm−1. From the 4*f*6*s* configuration of Pr IV, one finds [[1](#R1)] *ζ*4*f**=* 860.8 ±0.2 cm−1. The difference is due to a slight shielding of the 4*f* electron by the 65 electron in Pr IV. The same order of magnitude of this effect can be found in the comparison of the same configurations of Ce IV and Ce III [[8](#R8), [9](#R9)]. However, the value of *ζ*4*f* from La III [[10](#R10)] is slightly smaller than that obtained from 4*f*6*s* of La II [[11](#R11)]. This is probably due to a small perturbation in La II where configurations of the same parity are very close.

## 4. Ionization Potential

In [table 2](#T2) of the recent paper of Sugar and Reader [[12](#R12)] values of Δ*n*a = *n**a*(7*s*) *− n**a*(6*s*) derived from several 4*f**N**ns* series in the region of the rare earths are given which show that a value of Δ*n**a**=* 1.050±0.005 cm−1 can be used with confidence to compute the ionization energies of rare earths. The values listed are for singly, doubly and triply ionized species. With this value and the experimentally determined value of Δ*T= E*(7*s*)*−E(*6*s*) =125540.4 cm−1, the equation

| <!-- MathML: <math display="block" id="M15" overflow="linebreak"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> --> ΔT=Za2R[na(6s)]2−Za2R[na(6s)+Δna]2, |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

where *Z**n* *=* 5, was solved for *n**a*(6*s*). The corresponding value of <!-- MathML: <math id="M16" overflow="linebreak"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi>R</mi><mo>/</mo><msup><mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mstyle><mn>6</mn></mstyle><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> --> T(6s)=Za2R/[na(6s)]2, when added to the level value of 6*s* 2S gives the ionization potential as 463 350 cm−1. On the basis of the uncertainty in the value of Δ*n**a*, the value of the ionization potential is given as 463 400 ±400 *cm*−1 (57.44 ±0.05 eV).

In [figure 3](#F3), the error bar on the 7*s* 2S, Pr V point shows the extent of the possible change in the position of that point for a change in the ionization energy of the stated uncertainty. This gives us confidence that the value of Δ*n**a* used is valid for highly ionized rare earths.

## 5. Hyperfine Splitting of the 6*s* Term

The hyperfine splitting of the 6*s* 2S term of 2.95 ± 0.05 cm−1 leads to a value for the splitting factor of the 65 electron (*a*6*s*) of 0.983±0.017 cm−1. It is of interest to compare this value with *a*6*s* *=* 0.639 ± 0.007 cm−1 for Prill given by Reader and Sugar [[13](#R13)]. Relating these splittings according to the Goudsmit-Fermir-Segré formula, we get

| <!-- MathML: <math display="block" id="M17" overflow="linebreak"><mrow><msub><mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfrac><mo>⋅</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msubsup></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi> </mi><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mi> </mi><mtext>v</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfrac><mo>⋅</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msubsup></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext>Pr III</mtext></mrow></msub></mrow></math> --> [a6sZa2⋅na3dna/dn] Pr v=[a6sZa2⋅na3dna/dn]Pr III |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

Insertion of the experimental values in the above equation gives *a*6*s* (Pr V)= 1.03s ±0.032 cm−1, which leads to an expected splitting of 3.11 ±0.10 cm−1. This compares quite well with the experimentally determined value listed above.

Unfortunately, the interval between the energy levels also increases  $\sim Z_{\rm eff}^2$ , therefore, there is a risk to be out of the laser range. However, the Coulomb degeneracy and configuration crossing phenomena may help here. Indeed, in a neutral atom an electron energy level with larger orbital angular momentum is significantly higher than a level with lower orbital angular momentum with the same principal quantum number n.

For example, in the neutral Th the 5s electron is a core electron while the 5f electron is a valence electron. Respectively, the one-electron energy of the 5f electron is much higher than that of the 5s electron. Moreover, it is even higher than the energy of the 7s electron.

About 6500 lines are classified as transitions between 199 odd levels and 271 even levels. Of the 192 levels expected from the six odd configurations 5f(6d + 7s)2 and (6d + 7s)27p, 188 are now known. # IV. POSSIBLE METHODS TO EXCITE THE $5f6d_2$ LEVEL OF Th<sup>+</sup> AT 30223 cm<sup>-1</sup>

The experimental population of the $5f6d_2$ state of Th<sup>+</sup> at 30223 cm<sup>-1</sup> is, at first sight, not straightforward due to the difference of the total angular momentum with respect to the ground state: $\frac{15}{2} - \frac{3}{2} = 6$ . In addition, if one were to excite from the ground state using six resonant photon transitions, one also needs to introduce a change in parity, i.e., one of these transitions would need to have M1 multipolarity. In the following we therefore consider other possible ways to reach the level.

Firstly, the state of interest can be reached via three E1 excitation/de-excitation steps from the $6d_27s$ excited level at 6213 cm<sup>-1</sup> as indicated in the possible laser excitation scheme in Fig. 4.

content.text:
# 2 Atomic states and properties

Third-row transition metals in the periodic table of elements include Scandium (Sc), Titanium (Ti), Vanadium (V), Chromium (Cr), Manganese (Mn), Iron (Fe), Cobalt (Co), Nickel (Ni), Copper (Cu), and Zinc (Zn). Apart from Zn and Cu, they have partially filled 3d shells and their ground-state occupation of the 4s and 3d orbitals is often ambiguous. For example, the ground states of neutral Cr, Ni, and Cu have singly occupied 4s orbitals, while the rest of the atoms have doubly occupied

4s orbitals in the ground state configuration. The electrons in the 3d orbitals maximize their spin alignment according to Hund's rules.

The $4s^23d^{m-2} \rightarrow 4s^13d^{m-1}$ gaps (m is the number of valence electrons) of atoms Sc, Ti, and V correspond to the difference between the lowest energies of the states with spin quantum numbers $S_z = m-2$ and $S_z = m$ . For these atoms the low- $S_z$ state is lower in energy.

content.title: First-Principles Study of the Electronic and Magnetic Properties of   Defects in Carbon Nanostructures
content.text:
range of 8-6 eV. Subtitutional Ti presents the maximum binding energy, which can be easily understood since for this element all the metal-carbon bonding states (Santos et al. 2010b) are fully occupied. One could expect a continuous decrease of the binding energy as we move away from Ti along the transition metal series, and the non-bonding 3d and the metal-carbon antibonding levels become progressively populated. However, the behavior is non-monotonic and the smaller binding energies among the 3d transition metals are found for Cr and Mn, and a local maximum is observed for Co. This complex behavior is explained by the simultaneous energy down-shift and compression of the 3d shell of the metal impurity as we increase the atomic number (Santos et al. 2010b). 

In summary, the binding energies of the substitutional 3d transition metals are determined by two competing effects: (i) as the 3d shell becomes occupied and moves to lower energies the hybridization with the carbon vacancy states near the Fermi energy $(E_F)$ is reduced, which decreases the binding energy; (ii) the transition from Mn to late transition metals is accompanied by a reduction of the metal-carbon bond length by $\sim 0.1$ Å, which increases the carbon-metal interaction and, correspondingly, the binding energy.

The binding energies for noble metals are considerably smaller than for transition metals and mirror the reverse behavior of the bond lengths: 3.69, 1.76 and 2.07 eV, respectively, for Cu, Ag and Au. The smallest binding energy ( $\sim$ 1 eV) among the metals studied here is found for Zn, with both s and d electronic shells filled.

content.text:

So rather than working out the electronic structure of scandium by imagining that you just throw another electron into a calcium atom, with the electron going into a 3d orbital because the 4s is already full, you really need to look more carefully at it. Remember that, in reality, for Sc through to Zn the 3d orbitals have the lower energy - not the 4s...

The d-block elements: For reasons which are too complicated to go into at this level, once you get to scandium, the energy of the 3d orbitals becomes slightly less than that of the 4s, and that remains true across the rest of the transition series (hence, Figure 1 is incorrect as drawn). 

So rather than working out the electronic structure of scandium by imagining that you just throw another electron into a calcium atom, with the electron going into a 3d orbital because the 4s is already full, you really need to look more carefully at it. Remember that, in reality, for Sc through to Zn the 3d orbitals have the lower energy - not the 4s. So why is not the electronic configuration of scandium [Ar] 3d3 rather than [Ar] 3d14s2? ... Imagine you are building a scandium atom from boxes of protons, neutrons and electrons. You have built the nucleus from 21 protons and 24 neutrons, and are now adding electrons around the outside.

Now you are going to add the next electron to make Sc2+. Where will the electron go? The 3d orbitals at scandium have a lower energy than the 4s, and so the next electron will go into a 3d orbital. The structure is [Ar] 3d1. ... You might expect the next electron to go into a lower energy 3d orbital as well, to give [Ar] 3d2. But it doesn't.

content.title: Aufbau Principle - Transition Elements - Chemistry Dictionary
content.text:
The energy levels of an atom's electrons are influenced by a number of parameters, such as the nuclear charge and electron-electron repulsions. When there are fewer than 20 protons in the nucleus, the 4s sublevel is lower than the 3d sublevel. However, for 20 protons or more, 3d drops below 4s.

At scandium, rather than a valence electron configuration of 4s2 3d1, we get 3d1 4s2. This order is experimentally verified. For example, if scandium ionizes, it is the 4s electrons that are lost, not the 3d electron. The energy levels of an atom's electrons are influenced by a number of parameters, such as the nuclear charge and electron-electron repulsions. When there are fewer than 20 protons in the nucleus, the 4s sublevel is lower than the 3d sublevel. However, for 20 protons or more, 3d drops below 4s. Scandium has three valence electrons. The aufbau principle tells us they should add to the lowest available energy sublevel. Therefore, the first electron goes into 3d.

content.title: Electron Configuration of Scandium – [Ar] 3d¹ 4s² Explained
content.text:
Positioned in group 3 and period 4, Scandium mathematically organizes its 21 total electrons across 4 distinct energy levels.

The SPDF quantum orbital model explains Scandium's true three-dimensional structure. Dictated by the Aufbau principle, Scandium's 21 electrons populate spherical (s), dumbbell (p), clover (d), or complex (f) probability clouds in a strict energy sequence: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹ 4s². It terminates precisely in the d-block. Rendering Orbitals... ... The SPDF structure determines far more than just location; it defines Scandium's magnetic footprint, its ionization energy curves, and precisely how it physically overlaps with neighboring atoms to form complex covalent or ionic bonds. Our interactive SPDF diagram above allows you to see this subshell hierarchy mathematically stacked from lowest to highest energy states. Full Configuration: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹ 4s² ... Total Shells: 4 shells containing (2, 8, 9, 2) electrons respectively.



This describes the exact subshell occupancy following the Aufbau principle. Scandium is in the D-block because its highest-energy electrons occupy d orbitals.
